title: True stories of survival cannibalism!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore survival cannibalism through several historical cases: the 1972 Andes flight crash of the Uruguayan rugby team (Fairchild F-227 carrying the Old Christians club team, survivors eating the dead), the Jamestown colony's 'starving time' and the 2013 discovery of butchered remains of a 14-year-old girl nicknamed Jane, the 1884 Mignonette sinking and the killing of cabin boy Richard Parker (linked to Poe's Arthur Gordon Pym), the Alfred Packer case in Colorado, the lost Franklin Expedition of the Arctic and the tinned food and lead solder question, and the Siege of Leningrad. They close with listener mail questions about favorite foods, John Candy, Jerry's cats, Chuck's lost hat, ketchup origins, and running for office.
topics: Edgar Allan Poe Arthur Gordon Pym
Franklin expedition lead poisoning tinned food

segments.title: Opening banter and cannibalism disclaimer
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Chuck's dental implant, recall their earlier cannibalism episode, and warn listeners that the topic is graphic.

segments.title: Andes flight disaster and Uruguayan rugby team
segments.summary: A Uruguayan Air Force Fairchild plane carrying a rugby team crashes in the Andes around 13,000 feet. Passengers are sucked out, the fuselage slides down the mountain, and survivors face freezing temperatures with little food. An avalanche kills eight more, including the team captain. Survivors make pacts to eat the dead if they die, melt snow for water, and a few teens trek out to bring rescuers back. Sixteen survive. The hosts mention the 1993 film.

segments.title: Jamestown starving time and cannibalism evidence
segments.summary: Historians long suspected Jamestown colonists resorted to cannibalism during the 1609-1610 starving time. In 2013 archaeologists found butchered horse bones and a partial human skull of a 14-year-old girl nicknamed Jane in a trash heap. Three-dimensional reconstruction and isotope analysis suggested she came from southern England and arrived recently, and she likely starved, though disease may also have contributed. Colonists ate horses, dogs, cats, rats, leather, and by spring only sixty of the roughly three hundred new settlers survived.

segments.title: Mignonette shipwreck and Richard Parker
segments.summary: The yacht Mignonette sinks while sailing from England to Australia. Crew members, including seventeen-year-old cabin boy Richard Parker, drift in a dinghy. Captain Thomas Dudley kills Parker with a pen knife without a lot, and the survivors eat his flesh and drink his blood. They are rescued by the German ship Montezuma, tried for murder, found guilty, and released after six months. The hosts note Edgar Allan Poe's 1838 story featuring a character named Richard Parker who is eaten, and the same name used for the tiger in Life of Pi.
topics: Edgar Allan Poe Arthur Gordon Pym

segments.title: Alfred Packer and the Colorado cannibalism case
segments.summary: Alfred Packer, a prospector, leaves the Ute tribe in winter and later emerges alone, claiming the others died in a storm. His story changes under questioning, and personal belongings of the missing men are found in his pack. He escapes jail, is recaptured in Wyoming nine years later, is convicted of manslaughter, and is paroled after seventeen years. The University of Colorado cafeteria named after him and South Park's musical are mentioned.

segments.title: Break and dark meat discussion
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and briefly discuss why red meat is red and why dark meat differs from white meat in chickens.

segments.title: Franklin Expedition and lost Arctic ships
segments.summary: Sir John Franklin leads 134 men on an expedition for the Northwest Passage with five years of food, sealed in tins by provisioner Stephen Goldner, whose lead solder dripped into the cans. The ships Erebus and Terror vanish. Wreck of HMS Erebus found about two years before the episode. Inuit reports of starving white men and kettles with human remains suggest survival cannibalism. Lead poisoning theories are considered but bone analysis shows chronic rather than acute exposure.

segments.title: Siege of Leningrad
segments.summary: The Nazi siege of Leningrad lasted about nine hundred days, starving roughly 800,000 of the 3.3 million residents. Rations were tiny, and people ate substitutes such as cottonseed cake, glue, and wallpaper paste. Crime and cannibalism spread, with teen gangs and families hiding deaths for ration cards. Around 2,000 people were arrested for cannibalism, and 586 executed.
